page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: An element shows allotropy when it
exists in more than one form in the
They differ in physical properties such
steps.why: Three things make the definition complete: more than one form, the same physical state, and physical properties that differ while the chemical properties do not. Leaving out the physical state would let a liquid and its vapour count as allotropes, which they are not.
common_mistakes: Writing that allotropes are different elements. They are different forms of one element.
Saying the chemical properties differ. The chemical properties are the same; only the physical properties differ.
Leaving out the words same physical state. Liquid oxygen and oxygen gas are not allotropes — that is one form of oxygen in two physical states.
steps.memory_tip: One element, more than one form, same physical state.
steps.margin_note: Name the physical state inside the definition; it is part of the meaning.

steps.label: The reason and examples
lines: The forms differ because the same atoms
are joined or packed in different ways.
Carbon exists as diamond, which is hard
and does not conduct, and as graphite,
Oxygen exists as dioxygen O₂ and as
Sulphur exists in a rhombic form and a
steps.why: The definition on its own is a sentence a student can write without understanding it. Naming the cause — the same atoms arranged differently — and one worked pair such as diamond and graphite shows what the sentence actually means.
common_mistakes: Confusing allotropy with isotopes. Isotopes are atoms of one element with different mass numbers; allotropes are different forms of one element in the same physical state.
Giving oxygen and hydrogen as an example. Allotropes belong to one element, so O₂ and O₃ are allotropes but oxygen and hydrogen are not.
steps.memory_tip: Diamond and graphite, O₂ and O₃, rhombic and monoclinic sulphur.
steps.margin_note: One named pair of allotropes completes the answer.

insider_note: A complete answer defines allotropy in one sentence, including the words same physical state, and gives one named pair of allotropes such as diamond and graphite.
